standard.title: Decompose real-world problems
standard.description: Define and decompose real-world problems with design criteria and by creating user stories
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can define problems using given or co-developed design criteria and independently created user stories (AC9TDI6P01). They have not yet decomposed complex real-world problems into sub-problems or justified their decomposition decisions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students define real-world problems by framing what is known and what outcome is desired, decompose them into manageable sub-problems, and create user stories that capture user needs to guide the design process.

nodes.label: Framing a problem
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can frame a real-world problem in terms of what is known, why it is important, and what outcome is desired
nodes.minimum_width: Given a real-world scenario, state what is known, why the problem matters, and what a successful outcome looks like
nodes.typical_width: Frame a problem from a scenario that has multiple possible interpretations; justify why the chosen framing matters for the direction of the solution
wider: Apply problem framing to a context sourced from a First Nations community — how does the community's perspective shape what the problem actually is?
Investigate how problem framing affects solution direction — frame the same scenario two different ways and predict how each framing leads to a different solution

response_modes.reason: Problem framing requires students to make explicit what is known, why it matters, and what success looks like — three distinct questions that students commonly conflate or skip. Scaffolding the framing structure prevents students from jumping to solutions before the problem is defined.

nodes.hinge_reason: In a Mode B design cycle, every downstream phase (decomposition, user stories, design, evaluation) flows from the problem frame. A weak or absent frame produces decompositions that solve the wrong problem, user stories that don't connect to a defined need, and designs that cannot be evaluated against criteria.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The dual-framing direction (same scenario, two different framings) is a rich analytical task that reveals how problem definition shapes solution direction — genuinely deeper engagement than a single framing.
success_criteria: States what is known about the problem clearly
Describes what a successful outcome looks like

nodes.label: Decomposing into sub-problems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can break a defined problem into manageable parts by asking a series of questions and sub-questions
nodes.minimum_width: Given a defined problem, identify at least three sub-problems and explain how each contributes to the whole
nodes.typical_width: Decompose a problem into sub-problems with dependencies identified — which parts need to be solved before others; justify why the chosen decomposition is appropriate
wider: Use AI tools to assist decomposition of a problem and critically evaluate whether the AI's breakdown matches the problem framing — what did it miss or misinterpret?

Limited width — decomposition as a skill does not vary dramatically across problem contexts. The same questioning technique (what do we need to know? what depends on what?) applies regardless of domain.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three sub-problems from a defined problem
Explains how each sub-problem contributes to solving the whole

nodes.label: Creating user stories
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create user stories that capture user needs and use them as design criteria to guide the solution
nodes.minimum_width: Write at least two user stories in the standard format (As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason]); connect each to a sub-problem from Node 2
nodes.typical_width: Write user stories for different user types within the same problem; identify where user needs conflict and explain how design criteria help prioritise
wider: Create user stories from direct stakeholder input — interview a real user or community member and translate their needs into stories
Evaluate whether AI-generated user stories accurately capture user needs or introduce assumptions not present in the original problem framing

response_modes.reason: User stories integrate problem framing (Node 1) and decomposition (Node 2) by translating sub-problems into user-centred requirements. Students who write user stories without connecting them to their decomposition are completing a format exercise, not using stories as a design tool.

success_criteria: Writes user stories in a recognisable format that captures user, goal and reason
Connects each user story to a specific sub-problem or design criterion
